digest.intro: Fringe becomes policy, CSS becomes weapon, caves get dated, galaxies get counted.

items.title: The US-Iran pause rests on terms Tehran hasn't actually agreed to
items.blurb: Trump halted Iran strikes based on an unverified pledge to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end Iran's nuclear program — terms Iranian officials have not themselves confirmed. Meanwhile the US has 40 refueling aircraft in theater and is issuing embassy evacuation warnings, meaning Washington is visibly hedging against its own deal. The signal to watch: whether those aircraft begin drawing down in the next 72 hours.

items.title: The quieter Iran story: Saudi enrichment rights and what they do to the NPT
items.blurb: While Hormuz dominates headlines, the structurally more dangerous development is Saudi Arabia pushing for domestic uranium enrichment rights as part of a parallel US nuclear cooperation deal — at the exact moment the US is demanding Iran give them up. If Riyadh gets enrichment parity, it establishes a precedent that could trigger Gulf-wide proliferation and hollow out the NPT framework from inside.

items.title: How 'censorship-industrial complex' went from fringe meme to US foreign policy
items.blurb: In April 2025, Darren Beattie personally showed up to shut down the State Department's foreign disinformation tracking unit — staff were crying; elsewhere in the building, people were celebrating. MIT Tech Review and Type Investigations trace exactly how a specific far-right narrative about a 'censorship-industrial complex' moved from online fringe to official policy architecture, dismantling the institutions that tracked Russian and Chinese influence operations in the process.

items.title: QR codes that ARE dithered photographs, not just decorated ones
items.blurb: Andrew Taylor exploits the fact that QR scanners only sample pixel centers — leaving the surrounding space genuinely free — to fill the data module grid with dithered photographs that survive as scannable codes. It's not decoration applied over a QR code; the image and the code occupy the same pixels through different constraints. The result is one of those constrained-generativity projects that makes you want to immediately try it with your own imagery.

items.title: Extruding hollow tubes from a 3D printer using compressed air as the core
items.blurb: Jan at Roetz 4.0 built a dual-material extruder that wraps molten filament around a compressed-air line — producing hollow, inflatable TPU tubes in a single print pass. Pressure control alone proved too chaotic (thinning walls balloon until they burst); switching to volumetric control via a peristaltic pump finally gave consistent geometry. The output, when inflated, behaves like a soft pneumatic actuator — fabrication vocabulary that didn't exist before.

items.title: Laser-etched parchment paper as a circuit substrate with 250µm resolution
items.blurb: Zahra Rafiee et al. used a 50W CO2 laser to ablate the silicone coating on parchment paper, opening hydrophilic channels that accept conductive PEDOT:PSS ink — achieving 250µm line widths and functional RC filters on paper that composts in soil within weeks. The trick is working backwards from a hydrophobic base rather than trying to control absorption on a hydrophilic one. Fully degradable flexible electronics with off-the-shelf materials.

items.title: A Concorde fitted with telescopes chased the moon's shadow at Mach 2 to extend totality to 74 minutes
items.blurb: In June 1973, eight scientists aboard Concorde 001 prototype flew along the eclipse path across Africa faster than the moon's shadow, turning what would have been 7 minutes of totality into 74 — still the longest continuous solar corona observation in history. The route is still painted on the nose of the aircraft, now in a Paris museum. Worth reading three days before the August 12 eclipse, which gives observers in Europe just over two minutes on the ground.

items.title: The Vera Rubin Observatory just captured 650,000 galaxies in a single frame
items.blurb: Rubin's 3,200-megapixel camera — largest ever built — imaged the COSMOS field and resolved over 650,000 galaxies and 75,000 stars in one release, a region Hubble first photographed in 2003. The real payoff isn't the single image but the ten-year time-lapse: Rubin will revisit this same patch of sky continuously, adding the dimension of change to what every other telescope has seen as static.

items.title: CSS in your email client can steal passwords from third-party websites
items.blurb: Gareth Heyes spent months probing Yahoo Mail, AOL, Fastmail, ProtonMail, Gmail, and Outlook and found that CSS properties webmail clients explicitly allow — fully on the allowlist — can be chained to spoof UI elements, exfiltrate auth tokens, and extract passwords from third-party sites the victim is logged into. The attack surface isn't JavaScript injection (long-guarded); it's the styling layer that everyone assumed was safe. Elegant, uncomfortable, and very well documented.

facts.fact: The maximum duration of totality during a total solar eclipse is about 7.5 minutes at the equator — but a Concorde flying faster than the moon's shadow extended it to 74 minutes in 1973, a record that still stands.

QR code scanners only read the center point of each data module pixel, meaning everything surrounding those centers is unconstrained free space — which is how a dithered photograph and a valid QR code can occupy the exact same grid.

When 3D-printing hollow tubes with compressed air as the core, pressure-based control is inherently unstable — as the plastic wall thins, it offers less resistance and balloons continuously until it bursts; only volumetric control via a peristaltic pump produces consistent geometry.
The Vera Rubin Observatory's camera is so large that displaying a single one of its 3,200-megapixel images at full resolution would require hundreds of ultra-high-definition screens.

Saudi Arabia is currently pushing for domestic uranium enrichment rights in a US nuclear cooperation deal — at the same moment the US is demanding Iran surrender its enrichment capacity — which would set a precedent that could trigger Gulf-wide nuclear proliferation.

make_something.prompt: Generate a QR code that links to something you actually want people to find — then run it through a dithering algorithm (Floyd-Steinberg works well) applied over an image you care about, respecting the finder pattern corners. The constraint: the code must scan on the first try from a phone at arm's length. Document the failure states — the bubbled, burst, unreadable attempts are the interesting part, same as Jan's inflated TPU tubes.

art_picks.title: Tati's Playtime
art_picks.creator: Jacques Tati
art_picks.why: A film that is itself a generative system: a vast modernist set built as an interactive machine, where the 'story' is really emergent behavior from architectural feedback loops. The way Tati designs space to produce human comedy is the closest cinema gets to what you do with interactive environments.

art_picks.title: Unité (Habitation)
art_picks.creator: Thomas Demand
art_picks.why: Demand reconstructs Le Corbusier's Cité Radieuse entirely from paper and cardboard, photographs it, then destroys the model — a meditation on how images of utopia outlast the utopia itself. Obsessive craft, deep systems thinking, and a sharp question about whether the document or the thing is real.

art_picks.title: Replica
art_picks.creator: Oneohtrix Point Never
art_picks.why: Daniel Lopatin builds a haunted mythology out of sampled TV-commercial detritus — a generative system run on cultural sediment. It functions less as an album and more as an archaeological dig through collective unconscious imagery, the emotional inverse of the glossy surfaces it cannibalizes.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026 — Final Two Weeks
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St, Manhattan
events.why: The 82nd edition closes August 23 — curators Guerrero and Sawyer organized it around kinship and infrastructure, foregrounding 'mood and texture' over thesis, with works exploring technological affinities, shared mythologies, and the reach of US power through artists from Okinawa to Iraq to Vietnam; notably includes AI sculptures synthesizing social-media trails of dead artists into disjointed ghost-voices.

events.name: It's Alive! A Century of Animation from the Collection
events.why: Over 200 works tracing hand-drawn animation from 1908 to 2020 — not a nostalgia trip but a serious look at New York as the indie animation capital, from Dada film (Hans Richter) to early MTV ads, foregrounding the moment when drawing was still the only way to make something move.

events.name: Art of Noise — Closing Week
events.venue: Cooper Hewitt Smithsonian Design Museum, 2 E 91st St, Manhattan
events.why: 300+ works tracing how design transformed the human relationship to music — concert posters, phonographs, teenage engineering's choir installation, and Devon Turnbull's handmade HiFi Listening Room as a live sculpture you sit inside; it's a design show that is also a visceral sensory argument.

events.name: Pioneer Works Second Sundays — Summer Closing Day
events.venue: Pioneer Works, 159 Pioneer St, Red Hook, Brooklyn
events.why: Final day of three summer exhibitions including ANIMAL [a listening gym] — a free community day with DJs, food, and open studios in one of the best raw industrial art spaces in the city; today is the last chance to catch the summer program before the fall cycle begins.

events.name: High Visibility — Group Exhibition
events.venue: GOCA by Garde, 515 W 23rd St, Chelsea, Manhattan
events.why: Curated by Charlotte Hailstone Wu, the show uses color as a directed tool — examining how abstraction and representation shape perception and direct attention; a tight, conceptually legible premise from a gallery worth watching.
